analysis.one_liner: Launches a national program of thinning and salvage logging on federal forests to reduce wildfire risk, funded by a revolving timber fund.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced with zero cosponsors in November 1997 and referred to a Senate subcommittee, it died without a hearing or vote when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would order the Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management to run a nationwide program of "recovery projects" on federal forests — thinning, salvage harvesting, prescribed burns, and habitat work — aimed at roughly 35 to 40 million acres the bill says face high wildfire risk. It would set a scientific advisory panel, publish annual project lists, and pay for it with a new revolving fund fed by appropriations, leftover road-building money, a $50 million shift from firefighting budgets, and revenue from the timber the projects produce. It died in a Senate subcommittee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in fire-prone areas near federal forests would gain from faster fuels reduction, and local timber-dependent communities would gain jobs; the timber industry would gain a large new supply of federal thinning and salvage timber.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fire-prone communities and the timber industry

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Agriculture and Interior secretaries to begin a national program of recovery projects — thinning, salvage harvesting, prescribed fire, insect and disease control, and habitat improvement — in forest areas designated as at risk [S2] [S3].
It cites 35 to 40 million acres of Forest Service land at unacceptable risk of catastrophic wildfire and says the threat extends to human life, watersheds, habitat, and recreation areas [S3].

It would speed up forest inventory cycles, which the bill says are too slow (12 to 15 years) to give managers timely data, and require annual public decisions on project areas published in the Federal Register, with petitions allowed from any interested person to designate at-risk areas of at least 1,000 acres [S3].

It requires each project to comply with existing land management plans, bars work in wilderness areas and roadless areas under study for wilderness, and requires consideration of economic benefits to local communities [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the program through open-ended appropriations; leftover Forest Service road and trail money and $50 million from Bureau of Land Management wildfire operations would be redirected into the fund; and agencies would have to repay the fund out of their own budgets if projects missed the bill's deadlines.

drawbacks.text: The new fund would be fed partly by unobligated Forest Service roads-and-trails money and a one-time $50 million transfer from Bureau of Land Management wildfire operations, reducing money available for those purposes [S3].

The bill declares that several key program decisions — the standards for designating areas, the annual proposed project decisions, and reports to Congress — do not count as 'agency action' [S3]; under general administrative-law principles, decisions outside that definition are very difficult for citizens to challenge in court, so the most consequential designations would be largely insulated from lawsuits.

Strict deadlines come with penalties: if a project is not selected, started, and finished on time, the agency must repay the fund for all money spent on it [S3], which pushes managers toward speed over careful review.

The fund is replenished by revenues from the recovery projects themselves [S3], meaning harvest volumes that generate money pay for more harvest — a structure critics of 'forest health' logging have long said rewards cutting trees rather than the fire-risk work that doesn't.
It authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' annually [S3] [S2], an open-ended federal commitment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — treating overgrown federal forests that genuinely threaten communities with fire — has real merit, and the bill builds in audits, annual reporting, and compliance with existing environmental law and wilderness protections. But its financing loop (logging revenue pays for more logging), its hard deadlines with repayment penalties, and its carve-outs limiting court review tilt the program toward fast, commercially productive harvesting, and the open-ended appropriation would commit large public money with no fixed ceiling. Whether the fire-risk benefit outweighed those design problems was never tested, because the bill never advanced far enough to be debated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and then to its forests subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Gordon Smith of Oregon introduced the bill on November 8, 1997, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S5] [S1].
Two days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Forests and Public Lands, and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
No senator joined as a cosponsor [S4].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill expired without a committee or floor vote [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, federal forests stayed under existing management rules and no national thinning-and-salvage program was created; those who preferred the status quo on public-lands logging were spared the program, while fire-prone communities never got the treatment funding it proposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Backers of the existing forest-management status quo

for.name: Sen. Gordon H. Smith
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it was referred to committee

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat in subcommittee until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No partisan split can be observed: the bill never reached a vote, and no senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor.

industries.note: The bill would direct a national program of thinning, salvage, and other harvesting on federal forests, creating a large new supply of public timber, and would credit revenues from those sales back into the fund to pay for more projects — locking in commercial logging as the program's funding engine. Fire-risk reduction and commercial harvest would travel together, so the industry's gain would partly align with, and partly ride on, a public safety program.

The bill requires the agencies to consider economic benefits to local communities when selecting projects and to report those benefits to Congress, and project work and timber sales would flow through towns near the forests.

industries.industry: Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management
industries.note: The agencies would gain a dedicated revolving fund, an advisory panel, and new statutory authority for recovery projects, but would face hard deadlines with repayment penalties for late projects and limits on which of their decisions can be challenged.
